narrative:
The model estimates a 41% chance that you will leave your job. Because this probability is high enough to flag a risk of departure, the company has decided not to offer you the promotion at this time.

Three factors shaped this outlook more than anything else. First, your total years of experience across all jobs is only 1–5 years. Among people the model expected to stay, half had the same short track record, but the model still sees limited overall experience as a noticeable push toward leaving. Second, you have not received other job offers while working here. This absence of external opportunities actually pulls the prediction back toward staying, acting as a stabilizing influence. Third, you described getting involved in your daily work—sharing opinions and joining decisions—as difficult. This sense of limited voice is the strongest single factor pushing the prediction toward leaving.

Taken together, the model sees someone early in their career, without competing offers, yet feeling shut out of meaningful participation. These elements outweigh the many positive aspects of your role, such as having medical coverage, feeling some job stability, and reporting general satisfaction with the work itself.

The company should talk with you about ways to increase your involvement in decisions and give clearer paths for growth even with modest experience. You may want to reflect on whether gaining broader experience elsewhere could change your trajectory. Addressing these points openly could shift the outlook for both sides.
